claim: The study analyzed data from over 200 participants exposed to 1–7 languages across 36 languages.
source: Using data from over 200 participants exposed to 1–7 languages across 36 languages, we analyzed the role of language experience and typological distances between languages they spoke in shaping neural signatures of multilingualism.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the sample size and language exposure range.

claim: There is a negative relationship between the thickness of the left and right second transverse temporal gyrus (TTG) and participants' degree of multilingualism.
source: Our findings reveal a negative relationship between the thickness of the left and right second transverse temporal gyrus (TTG) and participants' degree of multilingualism.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Models incorporating phoneme-level information in the language experience index explained the most variance in TTG thickness.
source: Models incorporating phoneme-level information in the language experience index explained the most variance in TTG thickness, suggesting that a more extensive and more phonologically diverse language experience is associated with thinner cortices in the second TTG.
evidence: The abstract reports results from model comparison analyses.

claim: More extensive and more phonologically diverse language experience is associated with thinner cortices in the second TTG.
source: Models incorporating phoneme-level information in the language experience index explained the most variance in TTG thickness, suggesting that a more extensive and more phonologically diverse language experience is associated with thinner cortices in the second TTG.
evidence: The abstract presents this interpretation of the negative relationship finding.

claim: The pattern of negative relationship between TTG thickness and multilingualism is consistent across two datasets.
source: This pattern, consistent across two datasets, supports the idea of experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency.
evidence: The abstract states that the finding was replicated in a second dataset.

claim: The findings support the idea of experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency.
source: This pattern, consistent across two datasets, supports the idea of experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency.
evidence: The abstract provides an interpretation of the findings based on theoretical frameworks.

claim: Experience with typologically distant languages appears to impact the brain differently than experience with similar languages.
source: Our findings indicate that experience with typologically distant languages appear to impact the brain differently than those with similar languages.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Early auditory regions seem to represent phoneme-level cross-linguistic information.
source: Moreover, they suggest that early auditory regions seem to represent phoneme-level cross-linguistic information, contrary to the most established models of language processing in the brain, which suggest that phonological processing happens in more lateral posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG) and superior temporal sulcus (STS).
evidence: The abstract presents this as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Most established models of language processing suggest that phonological processing happens in more lateral posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG) and superior temporal sulcus (STS).
source: Moreover, they suggest that early auditory regions seem to represent phoneme-level cross-linguistic information, contrary to the most established models of language processing in the brain, which suggest that phonological processing happens in more lateral posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG) and superior temporal sulcus (STS).
evidence: The abstract references established models in the field.

claim: Auditory processing in humans with typical development depends on multiple regions within the temporal cortex spreading across the superior and lateral aspects of the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
source: In humans with typical development, auditory processing has been shown to depend on multiple regions within the temporal cortex spreading across the superior and lateral aspects of the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
evidence: The introduction presents this as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Primary auditory regions have been shown to be located in regions including the first transverse temporal gyrus (TTG), i.e., Heschl's gyrus (HG).
source: The superior aspect of the STG hosts tonotopically organized primary auditory regions, which have been shown to be located in regions including the first transverse temporal gyrus (TTG), i.e., Heschl's gyrus (HG) (Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites specific studies supporting this claim.

claim: The planum polare (PP) is immediately anterior to HG.
source: The planum polare (PP) is immediately anterior to HG, while the planum temporale (PT) borders it posteriorly.
evidence: The introduction describes anatomical relationships based on established knowledge.

claim: The planum temporale (PT) borders HG posteriorly.
source: The planum polare (PP) is immediately anterior to HG, while the planum temporale (PT) borders it posteriorly.
evidence: The introduction describes anatomical relationships based on established knowledge.

claim: TTG shows high variability in shape and size, with some individuals having one single gyrus, others presenting duplications or multiplication of TTG.
source: Of note, TTG shows high variability in shape and size, some individuals having one single gyrus, others presenting duplications (with a common stem or fully separated) or multiplication of TTG (Geschwind and Levitsky, 1968; Marie et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites studies documenting anatomical variability.

claim: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) lies directly below the STG and separates it from the middle temporal gyrus.
source: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) lies directly below the STG and separates it from the middle temporal gyrus.
evidence: The introduction describes anatomical relationships based on established knowledge.

claim: Understanding functional contributions of different brain areas to processing of sound and vocal stimuli has been advanced by lesion studies, ablation and resection case studies, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and intracranial recordings.
source: Understanding functional contributions of these different brain areas to processing of sound and vocal stimuli has been advanced by lesion studies (Hillis et al., 2017), ablation, and resection case studies (Hamilton et al., 2021; Hullett et al., 2022), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Booth et al., 2002; Da Costa et al., 2011; Humphries et al., 2014), and intracranial recordings (Hamilton et al., 2021; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies using different methodologies.

claim: No single functional parcellation of the human auditory cortical areas is generally agreed upon.
source: To date, however, no single functional parcellation of the human auditory cortical areas is generally agreed upon (Hamilton et al., 2021; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites sources discussing the lack of consensus in the field.

claim: Recent proposals of sound processing postulate that processing of speech is distributed and happens in parallel in different regions of the auditory cortex.
source: For example, in contrast to hierarchical models of auditory processing (e.g. Binder et al., 2000; Humphries et al., 2014; Scott and Johnsrude, 2003; Wessinger et al., 2001), recent proposals of sound processing postulate that processing of speech is distributed, and happens in parallel in different regions of the auditory cortex (Hamilton et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites a recent model contrasting with hierarchical models.

claim: According to parallel processing models, the posterior STG has been shown to be a crucial and essential locus for language and phonological processing.
source: According to parallel processing models, the posterior STG has been shown to be a crucial and essential locus for language and phonological processing (Bhaya-Grossman and Chang, 2022; Hillis et al., 2017), and to encode acoustic-articulatory features of speech sounds (Lakretz et al., 2021; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting the role of posterior STG.

claim: The posterior STG encodes acoustic-articulatory features of speech sounds.
source: According to parallel processing models, the posterior STG has been shown to be a crucial and essential locus for language and phonological processing (Bhaya-Grossman and Chang, 2022; Hillis et al., 2017), and to encode acoustic-articulatory features of speech sounds (Lakretz et al., 2021; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing encoding of acoustic-articulatory features.

claim: Primary auditory regions, including HG, have been argued not to be necessary for speech perception.
source: The primary auditory regions, including HG, have been argued not to be necessary for speech perception (Hamilton et al., 2021; Hullett et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites studies arguing against the necessity of HG for speech perception.

claim: Cortical surface area is relatively more influenced by genetics.
source: Indeed, a recent large-scale genome-wide association meta-analysis suggests that cortical surface area is relatively more influenced by genetics and that cortical thickness tends to reflect environmentally driven neuroplasticity (Grasby et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a large-scale genetic study.

claim: Cortical thickness tends to reflect environmentally driven neuroplasticity.
source: Indeed, a recent large-scale genome-wide association meta-analysis suggests that cortical surface area is relatively more influenced by genetics and that cortical thickness tends to reflect environmentally driven neuroplasticity (Grasby et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a large-scale genetic study.

claim: Environmental effects on cortical thickness might be tied to microstructural changes such as modifications in dendritic length and branching, synaptogenesis or synaptic pruning, growth of capillaries and glia.
source: Such environmental effect on cortical thickness might in turn be tied to microstructural changes to the underlying brain tissue, such as modifications in dendritic length and branching, synaptogenesis or synaptic pruning, growth of capillaries and glia, all previously tied to some kind of environmental enrichment and/or skill learning (see Lövdén et al., 2013; Zatorre et al., 2012, for overviews).
evidence: The introduction cites review papers discussing microstructural mechanisms.

claim: Increased cortical thickness may reflect synaptogenesis and dendritic growth.
source: Increased cortical thickness may reflect synaptogenesis and dendritic growth, while cortical thinning observed with MRI may be a result of increased myelination (Natu et al., 2019) or synaptic pruning.
evidence: The introduction cites a study on mechanisms underlying thickness changes.

claim: Cortical thinning observed with MRI may be a result of increased myelination or synaptic pruning.
source: Increased cortical thickness may reflect synaptogenesis and dendritic growth, while cortical thinning observed with MRI may be a result of increased myelination (Natu et al., 2019) or synaptic pruning.
evidence: The introduction cites a study and discusses known mechanisms.

claim: Previous findings point to an influence of experience-dependent plasticity on thickness of regions associated with speech processing, including the left posterior STG and left PT.
source: Previous findings point to an influence of experience-dependent plasticity on thickness of regions associated with speech processing, including the left posterior STG and left PT (Hervais-Adelman et al., 2017), as well as the STG (Mårtensson et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing plasticity in speech-related regions.

claim: Ressel et al., 2012, associated lifelong bilingualism with increased volume of the HG.
source: Moreover, Ressel et al., 2012, associated lifelong bilingualism with increased volume of the HG, a finding interpreted as reflecting experience-related plasticity related to the acquisition of novel phonology.
evidence: The introduction cites a specific study on bilingualism and HG volume.

claim: The main sample included 136 participants speaking between 1 and 7 languages (2.65 languages on average), representing 34 different languages in total.
source: The main sample included 136 participants speaking between 1 and 7 languages (2.65 languages on average), and representing a relatively wide range of linguistic diversity (34 different languages in total), see Figure 1 for a visual representation of the sample's language experience.
evidence: The introduction describes the main sample characteristics, with Figure 1 providing visual representation.

claim: The replication sample included 68 participants speaking to up to 5 languages, 2.44 languages on average.
source: The replication sample included 68 participants speaking to up to 5 languages, 2.44 languages on average.
evidence: The introduction describes the replication sample characteristics.

claim: Phonological perceptual space is known to be shaped relatively early in life.
source: Given the focus on auditory brain regions and on potential associations with language distance at the phonological level, and the fact that phonological perceptual space is known to be shaped relatively early in life (e.g. Werker and Hensch, 2015), we used information regarding the age of onset(s) of acquisition (AoA) of the different languages spoken by participants, and weighed each language by its AoA.
evidence: The introduction cites a study on early phonological development.

claim: High entropy values indicate more diverse language experience.
source: For this, we operationalized the language experience in a continuous and quantitative measure for each participant, using Shannon's, 1948 entropy equation (see Materials and methods, section 'Language experience'), with high entropy values indicating more diverse language experience.
evidence: The introduction explains the interpretation of the entropy measure.

claim: The cortical thickness of posterior STG would be related to the composite measures of language experience in multilingual participants.
source: We predicted (see Bhaya-Grossman and Chang, 2022; Hamilton et al., 2021; Lakretz et al., 2021; Mesgarani et al., 2014) that the cortical thickness of posterior STG would be related to the composite measures of language experience in our multilingual participants, and to the differences between their languages at the acoustic and articulatory feature level.
evidence: The introduction states a prediction based on cited literature.

claim: Multilingualism is hypothesized to be a dynamic process reshaping brain structure and inducing both increases (in initial stages) and decreases (in peak efficiency) in brain morphological indices as a function of quantity of the multilingual experience.
source: In terms of the predicted direction of these effects, according to most current views, multilingualism is hypothesized to be a dynamic process reshaping brain structure and inducing both increases (in initial stages) and decreases (in peak efficiency) in brain morphological indices as a function of quantity of the multilingual experience (Pliatsikas, 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a theoretical model of multilingualism effects.

claim: Acquisition of multiple languages is thought to have additive effects on brain structure and to induce cortical and subcortical adaptations to accommodate the additional languages.
source: Furthermore, acquisition of multiple languages is thought to have additive effects on brain structure, and to induce cortical and subcortical adaptations in order to accommodate the additional languages (see, e.g., Hervais-Adelman et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on multilingual brain adaptations.

claim: A positive relationship between the thickness of auditory regions and the degree of multilingualism would indicate that the auditory regions need to expand to accommodate the variability of phonological input.
source: A positive relationship between the thickness of auditory regions and the degree of multilingualism (weighted by greater phonological distance) would indicate that the auditory regions need to expand in order to accommodate the variability of phonological input in the environment; a negative one would suggest a specialization of the auditory system in relation to such variability (Pliatsikas, 2020).
evidence: The introduction provides a theoretical interpretation of potential findings.

claim: A negative relationship between the thickness of auditory regions and the degree of multilingualism would suggest a specialization of the auditory system in relation to phonological variability.
source: A positive relationship between the thickness of auditory regions and the degree of multilingualism (weighted by greater phonological distance) would indicate that the auditory regions need to expand in order to accommodate the variability of phonological input in the environment; a negative one would suggest a specialization of the auditory system in relation to such variability (Pliatsikas, 2020).
evidence: The introduction provides a theoretical interpretation of potential findings.

claim: The full main sample consisted of N=146 participants, with n=136 complete cases (Mage = 35.79, SD = 15.77; 85 females; 31 monolinguals) exposed to up to 7 languages (2.65 languages on average).
source: The full sample consisted of N=146 participants, with n=136 complete cases (Mage = 35.79, SD = 15.77; 85 females; 31 monolinguals) exposed to up to 7 languages (2.65 languages on average).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides detailed sample characteristics.

claim: The replication sample consisted of N = 69 participants, with n = 68 complete cases (Mage = 32.04, SD = 11.68; 38 females; 29 monolinguals) exposed to up to 5 languages (2.44 languages on average).
source: The replication sample consisted of N = 69 participants, with n = 68 complete cases (Mage = 32.04, SD = 11.68; 38 females; 29 monolinguals) exposed to up to 5 languages (2.44 languages on average).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides detailed sample characteristics.

claim: Across the two samples, the participants spoke a total of N = 36 different languages.
source: Across the two samples, the participants spoke a total of N = 36 different languages (n = 34 in the main sample, and n = 20 in the replication sample): Arabic, Bengali, Cantonese, Creole (Antiguan), Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Farsi, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hakka, Hebrew, Hindi, Hokkien, Hungarian, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Luxembourgish, Malay, Mandarin, Portuguese, Punjabi, Russian, Sindhi, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Swiss German, Urdu, and Vietnamese.
evidence: The Materials and methods section lists all languages represented in the study.

claim: The three distance measures (features, phonemes, phonological classes) were all related to each other, as evidenced by low to moderate positive correlations.
source: The three distance measures were all related to each other, as evidenced by low to moderate positive correlations between them, see Table 2.
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports correlations shown in Table 2.

claim: PHOIBLE includes phonemes and lower-level distinctive acoustic and articulatory features describing the phonemes for each documented phonological inventory.
source: For each documented phonological inventory, PHOIBLE includes their phonemes (see section 'Phonemes' below) and the lower-level distinctive acoustic and articulatory features describing the phonemes.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the PHOIBLE database content.

claim: Every phoneme in every language is described by 37 binary features in PHOIBLE.
source: Every phoneme in every language is described by the following 37 binary features: tone, stress, syllabic, short, long, consonantal, sonorant, continuant, delayed release, approximant, tap, trill, nasal, lateral, labial, round, labiodental, coronal, anterior, distributed, strident, dorsal, high, low, front, back, tense, retracted tongue root, advanced tongue root, periodic glottal source, epilaryngeal source, spread glottis, constricted glottis, fortis, raised larynx ejective, lowered larynx implosive, click.
evidence: The Materials and methods section lists all features used in the analysis.

claim: The cumulative phoneme inventory of a participant who was exposed only to English was equal to 40.
source: For example, the cumulative phoneme inventory of a participant who was exposed only to English was equal to 40, while an English-French bilingual's cumulative phoneme inventory would be equal to 64 (both English and French have 40 unique phonemes [Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019a; Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019b], with 16 phonemes overlapping across the two inventories).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides an example calculation with cited phoneme counts.

claim: An English-French bilingual's cumulative phoneme inventory would be equal to 64.
source: For example, the cumulative phoneme inventory of a participant who was exposed only to English was equal to 40, while an English-French bilingual's cumulative phoneme inventory would be equal to 64 (both English and French have 40 unique phonemes [Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019a; Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019b], with 16 phonemes overlapping across the two inventories).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides an example calculation with cited phoneme counts.

claim: Both English and French have 40 unique phonemes, with 16 phonemes overlapping across the two inventories.
source: For example, the cumulative phoneme inventory of a participant who was exposed only to English was equal to 40, while an English-French bilingual's cumulative phoneme inventory would be equal to 64 (both English and French have 40 unique phonemes [Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019a; Stanford Phonology Archive, 2019b], with 16 phonemes overlapping across the two inventories).
evidence: The Materials and methods section cites phonological archives for phoneme counts.

claim: Dediu and Moisik, 2016, proposed a comprehensive list of 167 phonological classes.
source: Using the PHOIBLE inventories and feature system, Dediu and Moisik, 2016, proposed a comprehensive list of 167 phonological classes, along with a method for selecting a language's phonemes belonging to given classes and computing their counts.
evidence: The Materials and methods section cites the source of the phonological classes system.

claim: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the PT, bilaterally, was related to participants' language experience at p=0.01.
source: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the PT, bilaterally, was related to participants' language experience at p=0.01, see Table 2.
evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings from the exploratory analysis.

claim: Participants with more extensive and diverse language experience had a significantly thinner PT.
source: Specifically, participants with more extensive and diverse language experience had a significantly thinner PT.
evidence: The Results section describes the direction of the relationship found.

claim: On average, participants had 2.375 gyri in the left hemisphere (SD = 0.63), and 1.84 in the right (SD = 0.64).
source: On average, participants had 2.375 gyri in the left hemisphere (SD = 0.63), and 1.84 in the right (SD = 0.64).
evidence: The Results section reports descriptive statistics from the TASH segmentation.

claim: The number of gyri was not related to participants' language experience, either in the left (β = 0.10, t = 0.97, p=0.335), or in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.01, t = – 0.13, p=0.90).
source: The number of gyri was not related to participants' language experience, either in the left (β = 0.10, t = 0.97, p=0.335), or in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.01, t = – 0.13, p=0.90), according to a linear model with number of gyri as dependent and language experience as independent variables (controlling for participants' age and sex).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical test results.

claim: Only average thickness of the second TTG (bilaterally) was related to participants' language experience at p<0.01.
source: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the second TTG (bilaterally) was related to participants' language experience at p<0.01, see Appendix 1—table 3.
evidence: The Results section reports the main finding from the TTG analysis.

claim: A cluster of vertices negatively related to participants' language experience at p<0.0001 (uncorrected) was found in the superior aspect of the left STG, corresponding to the location of the second TTG.
source: We found one cluster of vertices negatively related to participants' language experience at p<0.0001 (uncorrected), located in the superior aspect of the left STG, corresponding to the location of the second TTG, see Appendix 1—figure 5.
evidence: The Results section reports findings from the vertex-wise analysis.

claim: At the same threshold, no vertices were found in the right hemisphere, possibly due to greater anatomical variability in right compared to left auditory regions.
source: At the same threshold, no vertices were found in the right hemisphere, possibly due to greater, known anatomical variability in right compared to left auditory regions (Dalboni da Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section reports negative findings and provides a cited explanation.

claim: The model containing phoneme level information explained the most variance in the average thickness of the bilateral second TTG.
source: The analyses showed that out of the three language experience indices – (1) 'Language experience – features', (2) 'Language experience – phonemes', and (3) 'Language experience – phonological classes' – the model containing phoneme level information explained the most variance in the average thickness of the bilateral second TTG.
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results.

claim: The phoneme-level model outperformed the model containing the language experience index not accounting for any typological information.
source: It also outperformed the model containing the language experience index not accounting for any typological information ('Language experience – no typology'), see Table 5.
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results shown in Table 5.

claim: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, with a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively).
source: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, and had a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively), showing that the more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex (see Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical parameters and references Figure 2.

claim: The more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex.
source: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, and had a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively), showing that the more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex (see Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section interprets the statistical findings shown in Figure 2.

claim: The index of multilingual language experience accounting for lexical distances between languages explained less variance than the index incorporating phoneme-level distances between languages, both in the left and the right hemisphere (R2Adj = 0.164 and R2Adj = 0.116 for left and right, respectively).
source: We then entered this language experience measure accounting for lexical distances between the languages into linear models predicting the thickness of the second left and right TTG (controlling for participants' age, sex, and mean hemispheric thickness) and observed that the index of multilingual language experience accounting for lexical distances between languages explained less variance than the index incorporating phoneme-level distances between languages, both in the left and the right hemisphere (R2Adj = 0.164 and R2Adj = 0.116 for left and right, respectively).
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison with lexical distance measure.

claim: In the left hemisphere, the cumulative phoneme inventory measure explained variance in the thickness of the second TTG above and beyond language experience (β = – 0.004, t = – 2.910, p=0.004), with a small effect size (f2 = 0.06).
source: In the left hemisphere, this measure explained variance in the thickness of the second TTG above and beyond language experience (β = – 0.004, t = – 2.910, p=0.004), with a small effect size (f2 = 0.06).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings for the cumulative phoneme inventory analysis.

claim: In the right hemisphere, the thickness of the second TTG was not significantly related to the 'cumulative phoneme inventory' measure (p=0.76), when also accounting for overall language experience irrespective of typology.
source: In the right hemisphere, the thickness of the second TTG was not significantly related to the 'cumulative phoneme inventory' measure (p=0.76), when also accounting for overall language experience irrespective of typology.
evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings for the right hemisphere.

claim: The thickness of the left second TTG in these participants was related to the specific characteristics of languages at the phoneme level of their phonological inventories, irrespective of when these languages were acquired.
source: This result shows that the thickness of the left second TTG in these participants was related to the specific characteristics of languages at the phoneme level of their phonological inventories, irrespective of when these languages were acquired, while the thickness of the right second TTG was relatively more related to when and how many languages were learned (even though the typological distance information did improve the model fit, see Table 5), see Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—table 4, and Appendix 1 – (Second TTG and effects of language typology).
evidence: The Results section interprets the cumulative phoneme inventory findings.

claim: 40 participants out of 136 (29.4%) had a single TTG (HG) in the right hemisphere.
source: Yet, 40 participants out of 136 (29.4%) had a single TTG (HG) in the right hemisphere (versus only 6 participants, i.e., 4.4% in the left; see Table 4).
evidence: The Results section reports descriptive statistics shown in Table 4.

claim: In participants without posterior TTGs in the right hemisphere, the thickness of the first TTG was related to their language experience.
source: The analysis revealed that in participants without posterior TTGs in the right hemisphere, the thickness of the first TTG was indeed related to their language experience.
evidence: The Results section reports findings from the single TTG sub-group analysis.

claim: The language experience index accounting for most variance in the thickness of the first TTG was the index not accounting for typological relations between multilinguals' languages.
source: First, the language experience index accounting for most variance in the thickness of the first TTG was the index not accounting for typological relations between multilinguals' languages ('Language experience – no typology'), see Appendix 1—table 5.
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results for the single TTG analysis.

claim: The more extensive one's language experience, the thicker the HG (β=0.15, t=2.89, p=0.007; medium effect size: f2=0.237).
source: Second, the direction of this effect was inverse to that found for participants with multiple TTGs: the more extensive one's language experience, the thicker the HG (β=0.15, t=2.89, p=0.007; medium effect size: f2=0.237), see Figure 3.
evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: No significant relationship was found between the thickness of the PT and language experience in the sub-group of participants with a single TTG (β=0.02, t=2.43, p=0.81).
source: Of note, we did not find any significant relationship between the thickness of the PT and language experience in this sub-group of participants (β=0.02, t=2.43, p=0.81).
evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings for PT in single TTG participants.

claim: For PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16).
source: In addition, for PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16), suggesting that the observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only, see Appendix 1—table 5 and Appendix 1 – (Language experience in participants with a single TTG).
evidence: The Results section reports Bayesian model comparison results.

claim: The observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only.
source: In addition, for PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16), suggesting that the observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only, see Appendix 1—table 5 and Appendix 1 – (Language experience in participants with a single TTG).
evidence: The Results section interprets the Bayesian model comparison results.

claim: Language experience ('Language experience – no typology') did significantly predict the average thickness of the second TTG in the right hemisphere in the replication sample (β = – 0.13, t = – 2.05, p=0.046; small effect size: f2 = 0.087).
source: We again observed that language experience ('Language experience – no typology') did significantly predict the average thickness of the second TTG, but only in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.13, t = – 2.05, p=0.046; small effect size: f2 = 0.087), see Table 6.
evidence: The Results section reports replication findings shown in Table 6.

claim: In the replication sample, the language experience index weighted by phonological information at the phoneme level showed a better fit than the model without typological information, explaining 3% of additional variance in the average thickness of the right second TTG.
source: Furthermore, similarly to the analysis on the main sample (see section 'Second TTG and effects of language typology'), the language experience index weighted by phonological information at the phoneme level ('Language experience – phonemes') showed a better fit than the model without typological information, explaining 3% of additional variance in the average thickness of the right second TTG.
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results in the replication sample.

claim: In the replication sample, the model including phonological feature-level information had a better fit to the thickness data and explained an additional 14% of the variance (11% more variance than the model with language experience weighted by phoneme-level distances).
source: In contrast to the results of the main sample, however, this time the model including phonological feature-level information ('Language experience – features') had a better fit to the thickness data and explained an additional 14% of the variance (11% more variance than the model with language experience weighted by phoneme-level distances), see Table 6 and Figure 4C.
evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results shown in Table 6 and Figure 4C.

claim: No language experience indices were significantly related to the average thickness values of second TTG in the left hemisphere in the replication sample (β = – 0.03, t = – 0.53, p=0.60, and β = – 0.09, t = – 0.58, p=0.57, for language experience index without and with typological phoneme-level information, respectively).
source: No language experience indices were significantly related to the average thickness values of second TTG in the left hemisphere (β = – 0.03, t = – 0.53, p=0.60, and β = – 0.09, t = – 0.58, p=0.57, for language experience index without and with typological phoneme-level information, respectively), see Figure 4 and Table 6.
evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings shown in Figure 4 and Table 6.

claim: Multilingual language experience, quantified in a continuous manner, is related to the structure of the auditory cortex.
source: Multilingual language experience, quantified in a continuous manner, is related to the structure of the auditory cortex.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Multilingual language experience, weighed by the age of acquisition of the respective languages, is specifically related to the thickness of gyri (TTG) of the superior temporal plane.
source: Using two independent samples of participants, we find replicable effects showing that multilingual language experience, weighed by the age of acquisition of the respective languages, is specifically related to the thickness of gyri (TTG) of the superior temporal plane.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings from both samples.

claim: Typological distances between multilinguals' languages, in particular typological distance measures based on phonemes of the different languages (and to some degree on their acoustic and articulatory features), explains variation in TTG thickness above and beyond the effect of AoA alone.
source: Moreover, we show that the typological distances between multilinguals' languages, in particular typological distance measures based on phonemes of the different languages (and to some degree on their acoustic and articulatory features), explains variation in TTG thickness above and beyond the effect of AoA alone.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the typology findings.

claim: The effects are specific to the second TTG in people having at least one full posterior duplication, and to the first TTG in people having only one gyrus.
source: The effects we find are specific to the second TTG in people having at least one full posterior duplication, and to the first TTG in people having only one gyrus.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the anatomical specificity of the findings.

claim: HG is the first cortical relay station for auditory input.
source: The anterior-most TTG, i.e., HG, is the first cortical relay station for auditory input.
evidence: The Discussion states established knowledge about HG function.

claim: HG and the TTG as a whole exhibit large individual variation in shape and size.
source: HG and the TTG as a whole exhibit large individual variation in shape and size: some individuals have a single TTG, but duplications (complete or partial) and multiplications of the gyrus are also common, and have been observed both ex vivo (Geschwind and Levitsky, 1968) and in vivo (Marie et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion cites studies documenting anatomical variability.

claim: The TTG are known to be formed before birth, in utero.
source: The TTG are known to be formed before birth, in utero (Chi et al., 1977).
evidence: The Discussion cites a study on prenatal TTG development.

claim: Genes known to be involved in speech processing, in the development of the nervous system, and in X-linked deafness, have been related to the surface area and thickness of the left and right HG.
source: Further, genes known to be involved in speech processing, in the development of the nervous system, and in X-linked deafness, have been related to the surface area and thickness of the left and right HG (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion cites a genetic study on HG anatomy.

claim: Relationships have been shown between both HG volume and TTG shape (i.e. duplication patterns) and auditory and language abilities that are thought to be relatively stable and thus possibly arising from predisposition.
source: A body of work has shown relationships between both HG volume and TTG shape (i.e. duplication patterns) and auditory and language abilities that are thought to be relatively stable and thus possibly arising from predisposition, such as speech sound processing and learning abilities (Golestani et al., 2011; Golestani et al., 2007), linguistic tone learning (Wong et al., 2008), and general language aptitude (Turker et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites multiple studies linking TTG anatomy to language abilities.

claim: Studies have shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians.
source: Studies have also shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians (Schneider et al., 2005), and longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of this region is relatively stable over the course of a year (Seither-Preisler et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion cites studies on musicians and HG anatomy.

claim: Longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of HG is relatively stable over the course of a year.
source: Studies have also shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians (Schneider et al., 2005), and longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of this region is relatively stable over the course of a year (Seither-Preisler et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion cites a longitudinal study on HG stability.

claim: The bilinguals in the Ressel et al. study were not self-selected, so unlikely to have learned a second language because of a special talent for languages.
source: Importantly, the bilinguals in their study were not self-selected, so unlikely to have learned a second language because of a special talent for languages.
evidence: The Discussion describes characteristics of the Ressel et al. study sample.

claim: The findings of the Ressel et al. study suggested that the HG volume differences arose from experience with a different phonological system, since Spanish and Catalan are quite similar at the lexical level but have different phonologies.
source: The findings of the Ressel et al. study thus suggested that the HG volume differences arose from experience with a different phonological system, since Spanish and Catalan are quite similar at the lexical level but have different phonologies.
evidence: The Discussion interprets the Ressel et al. findings in light of language typology.

claim: Experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG.
source: More generally, our results show that experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG, and that increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's main findings.

claim: Increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
source: More generally, our results show that experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG, and that increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's main findings.

claim: Establishing that non-pathological environmental experiences are related to the morphology of TTG offers important insights into the adaptability of this early sensory region.
source: Establishing that non-pathological environmental experiences are related to the morphology of TTG offers important insights into the adaptability of this early sensory region, and has important implications for our understanding of the neural underpinnings of auditory processing in general, which we outline below.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the study's implications.

claim: The result aligns with recent findings of cortical surface area being relatively more associated with genetic factors and of cortical thickness being relatively more associated with environmental factors.
source: The result aligns with recent findings of cortical surface area being relatively more associated with genetic factors and of cortical thickness being relatively more associated with environmental factors (e.g. Eyler et al., 2012; Grasby et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites studies supporting the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Individual differences in the shape (i.e. duplication patterns) of the TTG seem to be related to how multilingualism will be accommodated by the thickness of the auditory brain regions.
source: Individual differences in the shape (i.e. duplication patterns) of the TTG seem to, however, be related to how multilingualism will be accommodated by the thickness of the auditory brain regions: increasing thickness of the first gyrus when no duplications are present, and decreasing thickness of the second gyrus for participants with more than one TTG.
evidence: The Discussion interprets the differential effects based on TTG anatomy.

claim: Accounting for typology (i.e. including information regarding how languages spoken by the participants differed from each other in terms of their phonological systems) explained more variance in the cortical thickness data of the second TTG than an index of language experience accounting for the age of exposure to different languages alone.
source: However, we observed that accounting for typology (i.e. including information regarding how languages spoken by the participants differed from each other in terms of their phonological systems) explained more variance in the cortical thickness data of the second TTG than an index of language experience accounting for the age of exposure to different languages alone.
evidence: The Discussion emphasizes the importance of typological information in the findings.

claim: Research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (distribution of DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and characteristics of phoneme inventory of language(s) predominant in that population.
source: It also has to be noted, however, that research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (distribution of DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and characteristics of phoneme inventory of language(s) predominant in that population (DeMille et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2020), and that genetic influences on auditory cortex anatomy have previously been observed (Cai et al., 2014; Guadalupe et al., 2014), making it possible that our results may in some part also be related to genetic rather than purely environmental factors.
evidence: The Discussion cites studies on genetic influences on language and brain anatomy.

claim: Language experience is particularly related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, and not to the rest of the PT, nor to other auditory regions such as posterior STG.
source: Our data show that, within the auditory cortex, language experience is particularly related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, and not to the rest of the PT (as shown in the analysis investigating the sub-sample of participants with a single gyrus in the right hemisphere), nor to other auditory regions such as posterior STG, as shown in the first, exploratory analysis across broader auditory cortex subregions.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the anatomical specificity of the findings.

claim: Tuning to the different acoustic-phonetic features might be an experience-independent feature of the posterior STG.
source: Tuning to the different acoustic-phonetic features might be an experience-independent feature of the posterior STG (i.e. it might be sensitive to features both present and absent from the languages a person knows), and therefore multilingualism might not induce any neuroplastic changes to this region.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the lack of STG findings.

claim: The findings may suggest that current language models might underestimate the role of early auditory regions (i.e. of HG and second TTG, when present) in phonological processing.
source: Alternatively, our findings may suggest that current language models might underestimate the role of early auditory regions (i.e. of HG and second TTG, when present) in phonological processing, and support their role beyond an initial spectro-temporal analysis of speech sounds.
evidence: The Discussion provides an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Fisher et al., 2018, has shown that speech sounds, and specifically vowel formants, are encoded in tonotopic auditory regions including HG and the STG.
source: Functional neuroimaging work by Fisher et al., 2018, has shown that speech sounds, and specifically vowel formants, are encoded in tonotopic auditory regions including HG and the STG, suggesting that even early auditory regions such as HG and second TTG (when present) are involved in speech sound processing.
evidence: The Discussion cites a functional neuroimaging study.

claim: Bonte et al., 2014 found that vowels can be decoded from fMRI signal of (among others) the temporal plane, HG, and sulcus.
source: Similarly, Bonte et al., 2014 found that vowels can be decoded from fMRI signal of (among others) the temporal plane, HG, and sulcus (see also Jäncke et al., 2002; Obleser and Eisner, 2009; van Atteveldt et al., 2004 for findings of processing of isolated phonemes in the HG and PT regions);
evidence: The Discussion cites multiple studies on phoneme processing in early auditory regions.

claim: Rutten et al., 2019, showed that attending to speech sounds (stop consonants) in pseudowords results in an increase in the neural processing of higher temporal modulations in regions as early as HG and also in the PT.
source: Rutten et al., 2019, showed that attending to speech sounds (stop consonants) in pseudowords results in an increase in the neural processing of higher temporal modulations in regions as early as HG and also in the PT.
evidence: The Discussion cites a study on speech sound processing in HG and PT.

claim: The finding of an association between greater multilingual language experience and decreased thickness of the second TTG may arise from increased processing demands (and associated cortical pruning) inherent to the acquisition and mastery of many non-overlapping phonological inventories.
source: It is therefore plausible that our finding of an association between greater multilingual language experience and decreased thickness of the second TTG arises from increased processing demands (and associated cortical pruning, see below) inherent to the acquisition and mastery of many non-overlapping phonological inventories.
evidence: The Discussion provides a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: Previous studies did not account for fine variation in the exact individual anatomy of the TTG (i.e. single versus multiplicated gyri).
source: Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, previous studies did not account for fine variation in the exact individual anatomy of the TTG (i.e. single versus multiplicated gyri).
evidence: The Discussion notes a methodological limitation of previous research.

claim: Based on the current results, the second TTG (when present) could be a possible candidate for preferential phoneme processing.
source: Our results may thus call for a re-evaluation of the specific anatomical site within the superior temporal plane in which phonemes are preferentially processed: based on our results, the second TTG (when present) could be a possible candidate.
evidence: The Discussion proposes a new hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: The replication sample included 31 individuals (i.e. 46% of participants) who spoke German and English, a language combination that has a phonological feature distance of zero.
source: Specifically, the replication sample included 31 individuals (i.e. 46% of participants) who spoke German and English, a language combination that has a phonological feature distance of zero.
evidence: The Discussion describes characteristics of the replication sample that may explain inconsistencies.

claim: In the replication sample, the phonemes-based typological distance measure numerically explained more variance in the thickness of the second TTG than a composite language experience measure based on AoA of different languages.
source: Notably, however, in the replication sample, the phonemes-based typological distance measure numerically explained more variance in the thickness of the second TTG than a composite language experience measure based on AoA of different languages, as observed in the main sample.
evidence: The Discussion notes consistency in the pattern of results despite statistical differences.

claim: The decreased thickness of the second TTG in relation to greater multilingualism may arise from functional remapping, experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, or learning-related increased myelination.
source: The decreased thickness of the second TTG in relation to greater multilingualism may arise from different, non-exclusive microstructural and physiological mechanisms, including functional remapping, experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, or learning-related increased myelination.
evidence: The Discussion proposes multiple potential mechanisms underlying the findings.

claim: Primary auditory cortex is known to lie within the anterior-medial part of HG (i.e. the first TTG).
source: Primary auditory cortex is known to lie within the anterior-medial part of HG (i.e. the first TTG; Rademacher et al., 1993), although there is no exact correspondence between cytoarchitectural and macrostructural boundaries (Rademacher et al., 2001).
evidence: The Discussion cites studies on the location of primary auditory cortex.

claim: In vivo markers for human primary auditory cortex include tonotopy, increased myelination, and decreased cortical thickness.
source: In vivo markers for human primary auditory cortex have been identified, including tonotopy, increased myelination (Dick et al., 2017), and decreased cortical thickness (Zoellner et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites studies identifying markers of primary auditory cortex.

claim: There is evidence that in professional musicians, functional activation extends to posterior TTGs during listening to musical sounds, while activation is confined to HG in non-musicians.
source: Also, there is evidence that in professional musicians, functional activation extends to posterior TTGs during listening to musical sounds, while activation is confined to HG in non-musicians (Schneider et al., unpublished findings).
evidence: The Discussion cites unpublished findings on musicians' auditory processing.

claim: Experience-induced pruning is essential for maintaining an efficient and adaptive neural network.
source: Experience-induced pruning is essential for maintaining an efficient and adaptive neural network. It reinforces relevant neural circuits for faster more efficient information processing, while diminishing those that are less active, or less beneficial.
evidence: The Discussion explains the concept of neural pruning based on established knowledge.

claim: Phonologically more diverse language experience requires that the mapping of acoustic signal to sound categories is denser, more detailed, and more intricate.
source: The cortical specialization may need to arise because phonologically more diverse language experience requires that the mapping of acoustic signal to sound categories is denser, more detailed, and more intricate.
evidence: The Discussion provides a theoretical explanation for the findings.

claim: Increased cognitive demand for speech perception may lead to neural plasticity, resulting in cortical specialization.
source: As a result, the brain may need to engage in more intensive processing to discriminate between and accurately perceive the sound categories of each language. This increased cognitive demand may, in turn, require the auditory and language processing regions of the brain to adapt and become more efficient. Over time, this heightened effort for successful speech perception and sound discrimination may lead to neural plasticity, resulting in cortical specialization.
evidence: The Discussion provides a theoretical explanation for the findings.

claim: Gyri are more likely to host specialized functions due to their greater neuronal density or to specific micro-anatomical features and connectivity properties.
source: Why this occurs in the second TTG and not in non-gyral portions of the superior temporal plane (i.e. in the PT more generally) remains to be explored in future work, but one possibility is that gyri are more likely to host such a specialized function due to their greater neuronal density or to specific micro-anatomical features and connectivity properties (i.e. greater proximity and thus more direct, local functional, and structural connectivity of neurons within the gyrus, as opposed to with neurons within the sulcal parts).
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the gyrus-specific findings.

claim: The neural efficiency account would be in line with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism, according to which the 'peak efficiency' stage of multilingual functioning comes hand in hand with reductions in local volume.
source: Either way, the neural efficiency account would be in line with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism (Pliatsikas, 2020), according to which the 'peak efficiency' stage of multilingual functioning comes hand in hand with reductions in local volume.
evidence: The Discussion relates the findings to an existing theoretical model.

claim: The supplementary analysis investigating second TTG thickness in relation to proficient versus non-proficient languages points to the tentative conclusion that the observed reduced thickness results might be driven by experience with proficiently spoken languages.
source: Of note, our supplementary analysis (see Appendix 1 – Effects of language proficiency) investigating second TTG thickness in relation to proficient versus non-proficient languages points to the tentative conclusion that the observed reduced thickness results might be driven by experience with proficiently spoken languages (more so than with non-proficiently spoken ones), aligning with the predictions of the Dynamic Restructuring Model.
evidence: The Discussion references supplementary analyses supporting the interpretation.

claim: Another potential microstructural mechanism underlying the thinner cortex result could be increased myelination of second TTG.
source: Another potential microstructural mechanism underlying the thinner cortex result could be increased myelination of second TTG; this would again be in line with the idea that multilingual language experience leads to modifications such that the second TTG becomes more 'primary-like', since HG is characterized by higher myelination.
evidence: The Discussion proposes an alternative mechanism based on known properties of HG.

claim: It has been suggested that the apparent thinning of the ventral temporal cortex during childhood is actually driven by increased myelination.
source: It has been suggested that the apparent thinning of the ventral temporal cortex during childhood (as argued by, e.g., Sowell et al., 2004) is actually driven by increased myelination, since increased myelination in deep cortical layers can shift the apparent gray-white boundary in MR images Natu et al., 2019; see also Mediavilla et al., 2022, for evidence on learning-related contraction of gray matter being associated with adaptive myelination in rodents.
evidence: The Discussion cites studies on myelination and cortical thickness.

claim: There might be different mechanisms underlying plasticity in regions more likely to contain primary versus secondary auditory cortex.
source: We speculate that there might be different mechanisms underlying plasticity in regions more likely to contain primary versus secondary auditory cortex.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the opposite direction of effects.

claim: It may be more likely that experience-induced pruning occurs in secondary compared to primary regions, and that in primary regions, greater efficiency comes at the cost of a neuronal 'bulking'.
source: In other words, it may be more likely that experience-induced pruning occurs in secondary compared to primary regions, and that in primary regions, greater efficiency comes at the cost of a neuronal 'bulking'.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for differential plasticity mechanisms.

claim: In people who do not have a second TTG, HG needs to accommodate both lower-level auditory processing and also the processing of more complex speech sounds.
source: Alternately but non-exclusively, it could be that in people who do not have a second TTG, HG needs to accommodate both lower-level auditory processing and also the processing of more complex speech sounds.
evidence: The Discussion provides an alternative speculative explanation.

claim: TASH provides a 'best-of-both-worlds' approach, by being anatomically precise while involving little manual involvement with the data.
source: Coupled with visual inspection of the data, TASH provides a 'best-of-both-worlds' approach, by being anatomically precise while involving little manual involvement with the data (which also tends to be error-prone).
evidence: The Discussion describes the advantages of the TASH method.

claim: TASH identifies more multiplications of the TTG than previously reported.
source: The measures we obtained align with the high degree of variability reported in previous literature, but they also seem to be more sensitive, since we identify more multiplications of the TTG than previously reported.
evidence: The Discussion compares TASH results to previous literature.

claim: In Marie et al., 2015, out of 232 subjects, 204 (88%) had one gyrus (including partially duplicated) in the left hemisphere, 28 (12%) had a complete posterior duplication.
source: For example, in Marie et al., 2015, out of 232 subjects, 204 (88%) had one gyrus (including partially duplicated) in the left hemisphere, 28 (12%) had a complete posterior duplication; the prevalence of further multiplications was not assessed in that study.
evidence: The Discussion cites a previous study for comparison.

claim: In the current data, a minority of participants (4%) presented only one gyrus in the left hemisphere, and most of them had either two (57%) or three (35%) separate gyri.
source: In our data, a minority of participants (4%) presented only one gyrus in the left hemisphere, and most of them had either two (57%) or three (35%) separate gyri.
evidence: The Discussion reports descriptive statistics from the current study.

claim: TASH identifies gyri based on anatomical landmarks and curvature values, and is surface-based rather than volume-based.
source: TASH identifies gyri based on anatomical landmarks and curvature values, and unlike previous descriptive work is surface-based rather than volume-based.
evidence: The Discussion describes the TASH methodology.

claim: TASH might be more sensitive to shallow cortical folds that might otherwise not be discernable in volume-based manual labeling.
source: It therefore might be more sensitive to shallow cortical folds that might otherwise not be discernable in volume-based manual labeling.
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for TASH's sensitivity.

claim: Variability in shape of the auditory regions is absent from other, evolutionarily older, species: macaques' auditory cortex is flat, and some chimpanzees have only a single gyrus.
source: Notably, such variability in shape of the auditory regions is absent from other, evolutionarily older, species: macaques' auditory cortex is flat, and some chimpanzees have only a single gyrus (Hackett et al., 2001).
evidence: The Discussion cites a comparative anatomy study.

claim: By showing that a human-specific experience, i.e., speaking multiple languages, is reflected in the anatomy of cortical regions that seem to be evolutionarily particular to humans, the study contributes to informing both models of neuroplasticity and of language evolution.
source: By showing that a human-specific experience, i.e., speaking multiple languages, is reflected in the anatomy of cortical regions that seem to be evolutionarily particular to humans, we contribute to informing both models of neuroplasticity and of language evolution.
evidence: The Discussion provides a broader interpretation of the study's significance.

claim: The findings support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages.
source: Apart from showing that individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations, our findings also support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages (Antoniou, 2019; Berthele, 2020; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion relates the findings to existing theoretical ideas with citations.

claim: Individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations.
source: Apart from showing that individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations, our findings also support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages (Antoniou, 2019; Berthele, 2020; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the findings.
